# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Finds Its Way Up

Water is heavy. This single fact explains almost everything about how municipal water systems work. A cubic foot of water weighs about 62 pounds, and every foot of elevation you want to lift it costs you roughly 0.433 pounds per square inch (psi) of pressure. When you turn on a faucet on the 40th floor of an apartment building, you're asking the system to hoist thousands of pounds of water more than 400 feet into the air—and to do so instantly, silently, and reliably. Here's how that trick is pulled off.

## The Physics of Elevation Head

Engineers talk about "head," which is simply the energy stored in water by virtue of its elevation. Water sitting in a reservoir on a hill 200 feet above your faucet arrives at your tap with about 87 psi of pressure before friction losses—free energy, courtesy of gravity. This is why cities historically built reservoirs and water towers on the highest ground available: elevation is a battery that never needs recharging.
